nodes.label: Sparda, Sardis
nodes.full: The Persian satrapy of Sparda took in Lydia, Ionia and Caria and was run from Sardis by a satrap who was usually a Persian noble or a royal kinsman: Oroetes under Cambyses, Artaphernes under Darius, Tissaphernes and Cyrus the Younger in the late fifth century. It was the western pivot of the empire and the base of its wars with the Greeks.
nodes.src: Herodotus 3.120, 5.25, 6.42; Xenophon, Hellenica 1–3; Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002).

nodes.label: Tribute districts
nodes.full: Darius divided Anatolia into tribute districts: the Ionians, Carians and Lycians paid 400 talents together; the Mysians and Lydians 500; the Hellespontines, Phrygians and Paphlagonians 360; and the Cilicians sent 360 white horses, one for each day of the year, and 500 talents, of which 140 paid for the cavalry that guarded Cilicia. The reckoning gives the economic geography of Persian Anatolia.

nodes.label: Royal Road
nodes.full: The Royal Road ran from Sardis across Phrygia, over the Halys and through Cappadocia to Cilicia and then east, with stations and inns at regular intervals and garrisons at the river crossings and the Cilician gates. The royal post covered in days a journey that took an ordinary traveller about ninety days on foot.

nodes.label: Paradeisos
nodes.full: Persian grandees laid out walled hunting parks and gardens — the paradeisoi — stocked with game and planted with trees, at Sardis, Celaenae and Daskyleion. The word, taken into Greek, became the Greek and then the Western 'paradise'. Xenophon saw Cyrus the Younger's at Celaenae and at Sardis.

nodes.label: Persian fire cults
nodes.full: Persian settlers in Lydia and Cappadocia kept fire temples with their Magi, whom Pausanias describes at Hypaepa and Hierocaesarea chanting from a book before an altar of ashes. The Persian Artemis, the Iranian Anahita, was honoured in cities of Lydia. The cult is known from later sources but reflects Achaemenid settlement.
nodes.src: Pausanias 5.27.5–6; Strabo 12.2.9, 15.3.15; Mary Boyce and Frantz Grenet, A History of Zoroastrianism III (1991).

nodes.label: Cyrus the Younger, Cunaxa
nodes.full: Cyrus, satrap of Sardis, raised an army of 13,000 Greek mercenaries and marched east against his brother Artaxerxes II, was killed at Cunaxa, and left the Greeks to fight their way home. Xenophon's account of the march begins in Sardis and crosses the length of Anatolia.

nodes.label: Xenophon’s Anabasis
nodes.full: Xenophon, an Athenian who joined Cyrus's Greek mercenaries, wrote a first-person account of the march from Sardis across Anatolia to Cunaxa and of the retreat through Armenia to the Black Sea. It describes Persian satraps, roads and estates, and the people of the land from Phrygia to the Pontic coast.

nodes.label: Gold for Sparta
nodes.full: Tissaphernes, and then Cyrus the Younger, financed the Spartan fleet against Athens in a series of treaties in return for the Greek cities of Asia. The money that paid the rowers of the Peloponnesian fleet came from Sardis. Persia decided who won the war.

nodes.label: Greek mercenaries
nodes.full: Satraps, dynasts and the Great King hired Greek hoplites in large numbers — Cyrus's 13,000, Memnon's 5,000, the 20,000 Greeks at the Granicus — and the market for soldiers fed Greece's poor cities. The mercenaries brought their skills and their stories of Persia home.
nodes.src: Xenophon, Anabasis; Arrian, Anabasis 1.14–16; H. W. Parke, Greek Mercenary Soldiers (1933).

nodes.label: Carian shield
nodes.full: Herodotus says that the Carians invented the helmet crest, the blazon painted on a shield, and the handle with which a shield was held. Greek hoplites had worn their shields on a thong. The claim records the Greek view of Carians as mercenaries and their reputation as soldiers.

nodes.label: The Granicus
nodes.full: The satraps of western Anatolia gathered cavalry and Greek mercenaries behind the river Granicus to meet Alexander. The Macedonians crossed under fire and routed them, and Alexander took the satrapal capital at Sardis and the Greek cities. The Persian defence of western Anatolia collapsed.

nodes.label: End of the Persian west
nodes.full: When Alexander crossed the Hellespont, western Anatolia had been under Persian rule for two hundred years. Most cities opened their gates; Sardis and Ephesus welcomed him, and Miletus and Halicarnassus resisted. The Persian satrapies were taken over almost unchanged by Macedon.

nodes.label: Daskyleion
nodes.full: The northwestern satrapy had its seat at Daskyleion on Lake Manyas and was held for generations by the Pharnacid family — Pharnaces, Pharnabazus, Ariobarzanes. Its governors dealt with the Greek cities of the Propontis and the Straits and fought the Athenians and the Spartans in turn. A seal archive of the satrapal chancery was found at the site.
nodes.src: Thucydides 8.6; Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.6; Daskyleion excavations (Kaan İren, Tuna Tuncay Bakır); Deniz Kaptan, The Daskyleion Bullae (2002).

nodes.label: Daskyleion bullae
nodes.full: Hundreds of clay seal impressions from the satrapal archive at Daskyleion record Persian officials and their business. The seals show Persian court scenes, Greek heroes and Anatolian subjects, and are the best material for the visual culture of the Achaemenid west.

nodes.label: Graeco-Persian stelae
nodes.full: Funerary stelae from the Daskyleion region show Persian dress and ritual — banquets and processions with horsemen — carved by Greek craftsmen and sometimes with Greek or Aramaic inscriptions. Such stelae, like the Çavuşköy stele, are the clearest picture of the Persian-Greek aristocracy of the satrapy.
nodes.src: Daskyleion excavations; Çavuşköy stele (Istanbul Archaeological Museum); Briant 2002.

nodes.label: Datames
nodes.full: Datames, a Carian by birth, rose from the king's bodyguard to be satrap of Cilicia and Cappadocia and a gifted guerrilla commander, minting his own coins. He fought the Persian generals sent against him, and in the end was murdered by a friend who had been suborned by the king. His career is the best-documented of a satrap who became a regional ruler.
nodes.src: Cornelius Nepos, Datames; Diodorus 15.91; Datames' coinage studies.

nodes.label: Satrapal coinage
nodes.full: Satraps, dynasts and cities minted silver in their own names: Tissaphernes, Pharnabazus, Datames, Mazaios at Tarsus and the Lycian dynasts. The coins, with legends in Aramaic, Lycian and Greek, are the best source for the local rulers and their pay of mercenary troops.
nodes.src: Babelon, Traité des monnaies; Datames and Mazaios coin studies (Alan Meadows, Peter van Alfen).

nodes.label: Horses of Cappadocia
nodes.full: Cappadocia was a land of horses, mules and sheep, the royal estates of which supplied the Persian cavalry and the king's table. The satrapy, with Datames at its head, was among the wealthiest of the central plateau. Its wealth was in animals.

nodes.label: Satraps’ Revolt
nodes.full: Datames, Ariobarzanes of Hellespontine Phrygia and others rose against Artaxerxes II in a series of revolts that Mausolus helped or hindered by turns and that ended with the murder of Datames and the failure of the others. The affair showed how far the satraps had become regional rulers with their own armies.

nodes.label: Kings of Cilicia
nodes.full: Cilicia kept its own royal house, with the title or name of Syennesis, which paid tribute in horses and silver and sent ships to the king's fleet, while the Persians kept a garrison. The king at Tarsus gave Cyrus the Younger money in 401 BC and, tradition says, hedged his bets with Artaxerxes. After the fifth century Persian governors, like Mazaios, held the land directly.

nodes.label: Cilician Gates
nodes.full: The great pass over the Taurus into Cilicia was a narrow cart road between rocky walls, which Xenophon says a single force could hold against an army. Syennesis abandoned the heights without a fight when he heard that Cyrus's officer Menon had entered Cilicia by another road and that ships had been sighted.

nodes.label: Cilician fleet
nodes.full: In Xerxes's fleet the Cilicians sent a hundred ships under the son of Syennesis and were reckoned among the larger contingents. Persia's western navy was drawn from Phoenicians, Egyptians, Cilicians, Ionians and Carians. A land power depended on the maritime peoples of Anatolia.

nodes.label: Hecatomnus, Mausolus
nodes.full: Hecatomnus of Mylasa was a Carian dynast appointed satrap of Caria, and his son Mausolus moved the capital to coastal Halicarnassus, rebuilt it on a Greek plan and expanded across Lycia and the islands, ruling with great independence of the Persian king. The dynasty's greatest monument is Mausolus's tomb.

nodes.label: Artemisia II to Pixodarus
nodes.full: Mausolus's widow and sister Artemisia held power for two years, followed by his brother Idrieus, his sister-wife Ada, and the usurper Pixodarus, who drove Ada out in 340 and held Caria until 335. His successor was a Persian, Orontobates. Ada kept the fortress of Alinda and was restored by Alexander.

nodes.label: Mausoleum
nodes.full: Begun by Mausolus and finished by Artemisia, the tomb stood about forty-five metres high with a podium, a colonnade of thirty-six Ionic columns and a stepped pyramid with a chariot at the top. The best Greek sculptors — Scopas, Bryaxis, Leochares and Timotheus — decorated the four sides. Its name became the word for a monumental tomb.
nodes.src: Pliny, Natural History 36.30–31; Vitruvius 7 pref.; Charles Newton's excavations (1856–58); Kristian Jeppesen, Halikarnassos reports.

nodes.label: Mausolus’s revenue
nodes.full: The pseudo-Aristotelian Economics, a collection of the money-raising devices of rulers and cities, credits Mausolus with a series of fiscal expedients, such as extraordinary levies and the sale of privileges. The stories show a dynast who had to find his own revenue for his projects.

nodes.label: Hellenising Caria
nodes.full: Under the Hecatomnids, Carian rulers used Greek architects and sculptors, wrote their decrees in Greek, moved their court to a Greek city and kept up Carian cults, while remaining satraps of the Persian king. The bilingual Carian dynasty is the best example of the cultural mix of western Anatolia.

nodes.label: Ada adopts Alexander
nodes.full: Ada, the dispossessed Hecatomnid queen, held the fortress of Alinda against Orontobates and went out to meet Alexander, offering him her cities and calling him her son. Alexander gave her back her rule, and she sent him cooks and confectioners. The adoption gave him a Carian heir's legitimacy.

nodes.label: Hecatomnid marriages
nodes.full: Mausolus married his sister Artemisia, and Idrieus his sister Ada, a custom of the dynasty that Greeks found strange and that fits the Persian practice of close marriage in the royal house. Artemisia's grief for her husband was proverbial and gave her the name of a model widow.
nodes.src: Strabo 14.2.17; Aulus Gellius 10.18; Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 3.75.

nodes.label: Lycian dynasts
nodes.full: After the Persian conquest Lycia was ruled by native dynasts — Kheriga, Kherei, Arbinas and, in the east, Perikle of Limyra — who were the Persians' vassals and also made war on one another. They set up inscriptions in Lycian and Greek, struck coins with their own names and built grand tombs. Perikle rebelled against Persia in the Satraps' Revolt.
nodes.src: Lycian inscriptions (Xanthos Stele); Greek Lycian coinage studies; Diodorus 15.90; Thucydides 2.69.

nodes.label: Xanthos falls
nodes.full: Harpagus, after the Ionian cities, marched on Lycia and the Xanthians came out to meet him and were beaten back inside their walls. They burned their wives, children and slaves and their treasures on the acropolis, then rushed out and fought to the death. Only eighty families, who were away from the city, survived.

nodes.label: Nereid Monument
nodes.full: An Ionic tomb on a high podium, ringed with reliefs of battles and banquets of a dynast and with statues of sea-nymphs between the columns, built for a dynast of Xanthos, probably Arbinas. It shows the Lycians commissioning Greek sculptors to commemorate Lycian and Persian-style rulers.
nodes.src: British Museum, Nereid Monument (Charles Fellows's excavations, 1840s); Pryce, Catalogue of Sculpture (1928).

nodes.label: Harpy Tomb
nodes.full: A pillar tomb with a chamber at the top, on which winged figures with women's heads and birds' bodies (called harpies, but perhaps sirens) carry off small figures, and on the sides are seated deities and gifts. The Lycian pillar tombs are among the most characteristic monuments of western Anatolia.

nodes.label: Letoon trilingual
nodes.full: A stele found at the Letoon in 1973 carries a decree of the Xanthians in Lycian, Greek and Aramaic, issued in the first year of Artaxerxes III under the satrap Pixodarus. It founds a cult of the Kaunian king and the god Arkesimas. The text shows the three languages of a Persian province.
nodes.src: Letoon trilingual (Henri Metzger et al., Fouilles de Xanthos VI, 1979).

nodes.label: The Letoon
nodes.full: Three temples of Leto, Apollo and Artemis stood together beside a sacred spring, with an altar and a nymphaeum, and made the Letoon the chief religious centre of the Lycians. Greek and Lycian inscriptions, a sacred pool and the statues of dynasts show how Lycian religion took up Greek forms.
nodes.src: Henri Metzger, Fouilles de Xanthos (1950s–); UNESCO World Heritage List no. 484 (Xanthos-Letoon, 1988).

nodes.label: Artemisia at Salamis
nodes.full: Artemisia, ruler of Halicarnassus, Cos, Nisyros and Calymnos, led five ships in Xerxes's fleet and advised him against fighting at Salamis. In the battle she rammed one of Xerxes's own allied ships to escape an Athenian, and was thought by the king to have sunk a Greek one. Xerxes said that his men had become women and his woman a man.

nodes.label: Artemisia the admiral
nodes.full: Artemisia ruled Halicarnassus as regent for her son and took five ships to Xerxes's war, where she advised the king against the sea battle and then fought it. Herodotus, a Halicarnassian, tells of her with pride, and has the Persian king applaud her.

nodes.label: Herodotus
nodes.full: Born into a family of Persian-ruled Halicarnassus, probably under the tyrant Lygdamis, Herodotus travelled the empire and wrote the Histories, the first long prose account of the origins and course of the Greco-Persian wars. His book, written in Ionic Greek, is the major source for Persian Anatolia.

nodes.label: Timotheus’s Persians
nodes.full: Timotheus of Miletus, a famed kitharode of the New Music, composed the Persians, a long lyric narrative of Salamis for lyre and voice. A papyrus roll of its text, found in a grave at Abusir in 1902, is the oldest surviving Greek book. A Greek of Persian-ruled Miletus performed it to Greek audiences.
nodes.src: Timotheus, Persae (Berlin Papyrus 9875, found 1902); Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff, Timotheos: Die Perser (1903).

nodes.label: Themistocles
nodes.full: The Athenian who beat Xerxes at Salamis, exiled and hunted, took refuge at the court of Artaxerxes I, who made him governor of Magnesia on the Maeander with the revenues of Lampsacus for wine and Myus for meat. He minted coins at Magnesia and died there around 459 BC.

nodes.label: Eurymedon
nodes.full: Cimon's Athenian fleet and army defeated the Persian fleet at the mouth of the Eurymedon and the army on the same day, according to Thucydides, and broke the Persian presence on the south coast. For a generation the Persians kept their fleets west of Phaselis.

nodes.label: Athenian tribute lists
nodes.full: The inscribed lists of the Delian League's first-fruits to Athena name hundreds of cities of the Carian, Ionian and Hellespontine districts, with their payments. Greek cities of Anatolia changed masters twice in a century, from the Great King to Athens and back.
nodes.src: Meritt, Wade-Gery and McGregor, The Athenian Tribute Lists (1939–53).

nodes.label: Carian battles
nodes.full: The Carians joined the Ionian Revolt and fought the Persians at the White Pillars on the Marsyas and again at Labraunda, and lost both times. Then, at Pedasus, they ambushed a Persian column and killed three of its commanders, Daurises, Amorges and Sisimakes. The revolt in Caria was put down in the next year.

nodes.label: Agesilaus in Asia
nodes.full: Agesilaus of Sparta invaded Persian Asia Minor in 396 to free the Greek cities and, after raids on Sardis and Phrygia, was called home. In 386 BC Artaxerxes II dictated the 'King's Peace', by which the cities of Asia were declared to be the king's.

nodes.label: The King’s Peace
nodes.full: In 386 BC the Persian satrap Tiribazus summoned the Greek envoys to Sardis and read to them the king's decree: the cities of Asia and Cyprus were the king's, and the other Greek cities should be autonomous. Sparta enforced the settlement, so that Persia became the arbiter of Greek affairs.

nodes.label: Ctesias
nodes.full: Ctesias, a physician from Cnidus in Caria, served at the court of Artaxerxes II for seventeen years and wrote the Persica in twenty-three books, from the royal archives, and the Indica. Only epitomes survive. He attended the king after Cunaxa.
nodes.src: Ctesias, Persica (Photius's epitome); Jan Stronk, Ctesias' Persian History (2010).

nodes.label: Hippodamus
nodes.full: Hippodamus of Miletus was credited with the grid plan for a city, with streets crossing at right angles, designed for Miletus after its destruction by the Persians and for the Piraeus. Aristotle, who lists him among theorists of the ideal state, calls him the first outside politics to say what the best constitution was.
nodes.src: Aristotle, Politics 2.8 (1267b); Hippodamus's Milesian plan (Armin von Gerkan, Milet reports).

nodes.label: Priene
nodes.full: Priene was moved to a hillside above the old Maeander gulf in the middle of the fourth century and laid out on a strict grid with terraces and a central agora and a temple of Athena by Pytheos, who also designed the Mausoleum. It is the clearest surviving example of the Hippodamian city.
nodes.src: Theodor Wiegand and Hans Schrader, Priene (1904); Wolfgang Müller-Wiener, Griechisches Bauwesen (1988).

nodes.label: Mosaic of peoples
nodes.full: Herodotus's list of Xerxes's army, with its Phrygians, Mysians, Lydians, Cilicians, Lycians, Carians, Ionians, Pisidians and many others in their own costumes, is the best map of the ethnic variety of Persian Anatolia. The empire left its peoples their languages and gods and put satraps and garrisons above them.

nodes.label: Cyrus takes Lydia
nodes.full: Cyrus of Persia took Sardis around 546 BC and his general Harpagus then subdued the Greek cities and the peoples of the coast, which made western Anatolia a Persian province.
nodes.src: background — see the Lydia folio (lydia-685bc-546bc) and the Greek Ionia folio (ionia-1050bc-494bc)

nodes.label: The fall of Miletus
nodes.full: The Persian fleet defeated the Ionians at Lade in 494 BC and Miletus was sacked and its people deported.
nodes.src: background — see the Greek Ionia folio (ionia-1050bc-494bc)
